To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the Miocene proboscidean, Gomphothrium, was a mixed feeder with C3 biomass as the primary dietary constituent and C4 biomass comprising no more than 50% of the diet, and that the diet did not include more C4 biomass through the Miocene.

Gomphotheri um was a C3 browser or mixed feeder, that there was no change in the diet of this species through the Miocene, that there was a geographic difference in the diet of the species, and that wooded habitat was available to support large herbivores in the Great Plains during the Miocene.

Gomphotherum, a Miocene proboscidean, was a C 4 browser or mixed feeder with a bias toward browse and that areas of wooded or forested habitat sufficient to support large-bodied herbivore herds remained available in the central Great Plains through the late Miocene.

the reconstruction of the diet and habitat use of a large mammal from the Great Plains of the US during the Late Miocene, based on the stable carbon isotope composition in tooth enamel.

Gomphotheres, as a group, are not good proxies for paleoenvironmental reconstructions.
Gomphotheriidae were not the only herbivores that could live on C 3 plants in arid regions, but they were the most abundant and widespread of these herbivores.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in spite of the presence of C 4 plants in the Great Plains during the Middle Miocene, Gomphtherium was not a mixed feeder with C 4 plants as a primary component of the diet.
Gomphotheriids, like other Proboscideans, were browsers and not grazers, as is often assumed in paleoecological reconstructions.

the carbon isotope compositions of tusk enamel are useful for dietary reconstruction in proboscideans, and the carbon isotope values of tusk enamel can be used to infer the proportion of C 3 and/or C 4 plants in the diet of proboscideans.
